passage:
Sunday. Arohi told her two closest friends what had happened, over tea in the corridor. Neither tried to fix it. One said, "Come to the canteen tomorrow." Arohi did not want to go, but she went, and sat quiet while they talked about a film.
Wednesday. An invitation to a birthday dinner came. She almost said no. She wrote "yes" and went, and left early, and no one minded. That night, she phoned her sister Ritu, as she now did every week.
Saturday. Ritu said, "You sound less flat." Arohi noticed it too. The week had not been good, but it had not been lonely, and that was a different kind of hard.

qa.q: Which day did Arohi phone her sister Ritu?
qa.a: Arohi phoned her sister Ritu on Wednesday night.

qa.q: What did Arohi feel when the birthday dinner invitation came?
qa.a: Arohi almost said no, so she felt reluctant and unwilling, but she chose to go anyway.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Arohi add, and why?
qa.a: Arohi could plan one small activity she used to enjoy, because company helps but a familiar activity can also bring back some ease.

qa.q: How does Ritu see Arohi's week?
qa.a: Ritu hears the weekly call and says Arohi sounds less flat, so Ritu can tell from her voice that the support is helping a little.

grounding: Shows leaning on friends and family after a breakup by talking, accepting invitations even when unwilling, and a weekly call.

passage:
Vaibhav, you've said no to every plan for three weeks. Let me, your Tejas mama, tell you what I did when I was twenty and my first relationship ended.
For four days I stayed in my hostel room and told everyone I had fever. Then my roommate Irfan knocked and wouldn't leave. So I told him, and my friend Suresh too. Just the two of them, the whole thing.
After that I made one rule: if someone invites me, I go, even if I sit in the corner. I went to a cricket match where I didn't watch a single ball. I went to Suresh's cousin's wedding and ate too much. And every Sunday I called my sister in Nagpur, even if I only said 'fine'.
It didn't make the pain go. It stopped it from growing in that small room.
So. There's a dinner at your aunt's on Saturday. You're coming with me.

qa.q: Who did Tejas tell about the breakup?
qa.a: His roommate Irfan, and his friend Suresh too.

qa.q: How was Tejas feeling during the four days in the hostel room?
qa.a: He felt lonely and hurt, hiding behind a fake fever instead of telling anyone.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the biggest difference?
qa.a: Letting Irfan in and then making the rule to accept every invitation, even when not in the mood, which stopped the isolation.

qa.q: How might Irfan have seen those four days?
qa.a: Irfan likely sensed the fever story didn't add up and felt worried enough to knock and stay.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling telling two friends, going to every invitation and calling a sibling weekly after a breakup, so isolation did not deepen the pain.

passage:
The breakup came two weeks into Vidya's internship in Hyderabad, a city where she knew almost no one. Her paying-guest room had a window facing a wall, and by the third evening she had stopped switching the light on.
On the fourth evening she made herself message the two people she trusted most, her school friends Fiza and Anu, in a group chat: 'We broke up. I'm not okay.' Fiza called within five minutes.
She made a small plan after that. When the other interns asked her to biryani night on Friday, she said yes, though she wanted to say no. She sat quietly, but she laughed once. And she set a call with her brother Gautam in Bhubaneswar, every Sunday at seven.
On the third Sunday Gautam said, 'You sound more like yourself.' She did. The room still faced a wall, but the light was on.

qa.q: When is Vidya's call with Gautam?
What was Vidya feeling when she stopped switching the light on?
qa.a: She felt lonely and low, alone in a new city right after the breakup.

qa.q: What else could Vidya do if weekday evenings stay hard?
qa.a: Plan one small thing with people on a weekday too, like a walk with another intern, so not only Fridays and Sundays have company.

qa.q: How does Gautam experience the Sunday calls?
qa.a: Gautam hears his sister gradually coming back, and by the third Sunday tells her she sounds more like herself.

grounding: Shows a student alone in a new city telling two close friends, accepting invitations and calling a sibling weekly after a breakup, which eases the isolation.
